title: Networking: packets, addresses, ports
story:
A message has to reach a program on another machine, crossing networks that were not designed together and are run by people who have never spoken. Three ideas carry the whole arrangement, and each answers a different question.

Cut the message into packets, because the alternative is reserving a path for the duration and that does not share. Packets from unrelated conversations interleave on the same wire, each carrying enough information to be handled alone. The consequence is that any packet may be dropped when something is congested, may take a different route from its neighbour, and may therefore arrive out of order or not at all.

Give every network interface an address, so a packet can be routed by machines that know nothing about it except where it is going. No router holds a map of the whole network; each knows only the next step. That is what lets the arrangement scale to networks nobody administers centrally.

Then give every conversation on a machine a second number, a port, so that an arriving packet can be handed to the right program. The address gets it to the machine; the port gets it to the process. Two numbers, two different questions, and conflating them is the most common confusion here.

What sits above is the interesting part. The specification published as RFC 793 in September 1981 is explicit about how little it assumes underneath: it makes very few assumptions about the reliability of the layers below, assuming only a simple, potentially unreliable datagram service, and states it should in principle operate above a wide spectrum of communication systems ranging from hard-wired connections to packet-switched or circuit-switched networks. Every guarantee you associate with a reliable connection — ordering, retransmission, duplicate detection, flow control — is built on top of a layer that promises none of them.

That layering is why the advice from the storage lesson reappears. Guarantees are constructed from acknowledgements, and acknowledgements are round trips, and round trips are latency — the quantity that improves least. A protocol that needs three exchanges before carrying data costs three times the distance to the other end, regardless of how wide the pipe is.

One sourcing note worth carrying, since this document is cited constantly: RFC 793 was itself the ninth edition of the specification, and it was obsoleted by RFC 9293 in 2022. The number most engineers quote for this protocol has not been the current specification for several years.

problem.name: Packet switching
problem.shape: A message must reach a specific program on a machine you do not control, across networks that were not built together.
tell: a protocol is being designed over an unreliable link
ordering or delivery is being assumed rather than arranged
a conversation needs to be distinguished from others to the same host
round trips are being added to a request path
problem.move: Separate the three questions: which machine, which program, and what guarantees you need. Build only the guarantees you require, because each one costs round trips, and count those round trips as the primary cost of any protocol you design.
problem.invariant: The layer beneath promises nothing — packets may be dropped, duplicated, reordered or delayed. Every reliability property above it is constructed, and construction means acknowledgements.
problem.breaks: Reliability is constructed per connection, so it guarantees delivery to the other end's protocol stack rather than to the other end's application. A message that was acknowledged may still have been lost after acknowledgement, which is why idempotency and retries are a separate lesson rather than a solved problem here.

cost.time: round trips, which is latency, which is the quantity that improves least over time
cost.space: per-connection state at both ends, which is the thing connection pooling later exists to amortise
cost.beats: reserving a dedicated path per conversation, which guarantees delivery and cannot share the wire

worked.problem: What does an address identify, and what does a port identify?
worked.reasoning:
Different things, and the distinction is the reason both exist.

An address identifies a network interface — a place on the network that packets can be routed to. It is what the intermediate machines use, and they use nothing else: a router does not know what your packet contains or which program will receive it, only which direction to send it next. That is deliberate, because it means no router needs a map of the whole network, which is what allows a network with no central administrator to work at all.

A port identifies a conversation endpoint within a machine. Once packets arrive, the receiving machine has many programs and needs to know which one asked for this. The port is that discriminator. It is meaningless outside the machine and the routers never inspect it.

So the address answers which machine and the port answers which program, and a connection is identified by more than either — in practice by the pair of addresses and the pair of ports together, which is what lets one machine hold many simultaneous conversations with the same remote host without confusing them.

The layering point underneath is the one worth carrying. The transport specification says explicitly that it makes very few assumptions about the reliability of the layers below, assuming only a simple, potentially unreliable datagram service, and should operate above a wide spectrum of communication systems. So everything you associate with a reliable connection — ordering, retransmission, duplicate detection, flow control — is built above a layer that guarantees none of it.

And the practical consequence: those guarantees are made of acknowledgements, acknowledgements are round trips, and round trips are latency. A protocol needing three exchanges before it carries data costs three times the distance to the other end no matter how wide the pipe is. That is the same conclusion as the storage lesson and it arrives for the same reason.

One thing I would add unprompted, because people over-trust it: this reliability is between the two protocol stacks, not between the two applications. An acknowledged message can still be lost after acknowledgement — the receiving process may crash before handling it. Which is why idempotency and retries are their own problem rather than something the transport solved.

problem.practice: Take a request your system makes to another service and count the round trips before the first useful byte moves — connection setup, security negotiation, then the request itself. Multiply by the round-trip time to that service. Compare the result to the time the service spends doing the work.

beats.broke: A message must cross machines and networks that were not built together, may be dropped or reordered, and have no common notion of who anything is.
beats.fix: Cut the message into independently addressed packets, give every interface a number so packets can be routed, and give every conversation a second number so arriving packets reach the right program.
beats.cost: The layer beneath guarantees nothing, so ordering, retransmission and duplicate detection are built above it — and every such guarantee is paid for in round trips.

interview.q: What does an address identify, and what does a port identify?
interview.trap: Treating them as two halves of one identifier. They answer different questions for different parties — routers use the address and never inspect the port, and a connection is identified by both pairs together rather than by either.
interview.answer:
Different things, and that is why both exist.

An address identifies a network interface — a place packets can be routed to. It is what intermediate machines use and all they use: a router does not know what the packet contains or which program will receive it, only which direction to send it next. That is deliberate, because it means no router needs a map of the whole network, which is what lets a network with no central administrator function.

A port identifies a conversation endpoint within a machine. Once packets arrive the receiving machine has many programs and needs to know which asked for this; the port is that discriminator, meaningless outside the machine and never inspected by routers.

So address answers which machine, port answers which program — and a connection is identified by more than either, in practice by both addresses and both ports, which is what lets one machine hold many simultaneous conversations with the same host.

The layering underneath is the part worth carrying. The transport specification says it makes very few assumptions about the reliability of the layers below, assuming only a simple, potentially unreliable datagram service. So ordering, retransmission, duplicate detection and flow control are all constructed above a layer guaranteeing none of them.

And the consequence: those guarantees are made of acknowledgements, acknowledgements are round trips, round trips are latency. A protocol needing three exchanges before carrying data costs three times the distance regardless of pipe width.

One thing I would add because people over-trust it — this reliability is between the two protocol stacks, not the two applications. An acknowledged message can still be lost afterwards if the receiving process crashes before handling it, which is why idempotency and retries are a separate problem.
